Intrinsic alignments (IA) of galaxies represent a significant source of systematic uncertainty in weak lensing studies. This work investigates how scalar-field dark energy models, specifically within the Horndeski framework, influence IA. We examine two distinct Horndeski scenarios: one where the scalar field interacts with the electromagnetic field, and another where it couples to matter. Our findings indicate that the Horndeski models produce a negligible impact on the IA signal, a conclusion that remains robust even when accounting for galaxy shape measurement noise. Consequently, the combination of cosmic shear and intrinsic alignments offers a viable method for constraining the parameters of these models.

This study investigates the rheological behavior of systems composed of deformable spheres, utilizing both theoretical frameworks and molecular dynamics simulations. We analyze the rheology of deformable particles in two distinct regimes: those that undergo elastic deformation and those that experience plastic deformation. Our findings indicate that the zero-shear viscosity of a dilute suspension of rigid, elastic particles is governed by the magnitude of the applied force required to initiate deformation. Conversely, in the plastic deformation regime, the viscosity is determined by the average dissipation occurring during particle collisions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the viscosity of a dilute suspension of rigid, incompressible particles is governed by the rate at which work is performed to compress them.

This study presents a data-driven simulation of gold nanoparticle melting, utilizing a recently developed, highly accurate interatomic potential. The findings reveal that melting occurs abruptly at a specific temperature, which remains independent of the particle's size. Furthermore, the enthalpy of fusion is found to be constant at approximately 1.26 kJ/mol, aligning with bulk gold values. These results are corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations, which demonstrate that the nanoparticle's structural evolution during thermal excitation can be accurately modeled using a recently formulated, highly precise interatomic potential.

This two-part study introduces a novel framework for analyzing bifurcations and splitting phenomena within potential operators that lack smoothness. The first section establishes the foundational concepts and provides a comprehensive overview of the second section, which is dedicated to this work.

The fundamental question of why there are exactly three generations of leptons and six types of quarks remains unresolved. This study introduces a theoretical framework based on the geometry of a tetrahedron, where each face represents a generation, and applies it to explain the observed particle counts. By establishing a correspondence between this four-vertex structure and the mathematical concept of the 3-color problem, we demonstrate that both systems inherently require exactly three distinct categories. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this model for the discovery of a fourth generation of fermions.

This paper presents a comprehensive study of the (h,q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials, which are defined through p-adic forward difference operators. Furthermore, we derive a fundamental identity for these objects and explore their properties in depth.

This paper introduces a new reinforcement learning approach for estimating the long-term impacts of treatments. By utilizing a sequence of fitted Q factorization algorithms, we generate a series of policies that are both non-stationary and non-Markovian, specifically designed to maximize cumulative rewards over a fixed horizon. We demonstrate that this method provides a consistent estimator for the long-term treatment effect, even when the underlying data distribution is unknown. Additionally, we examine the convergence rate of the proposed estimator and validate our findings through a simulation study.

Case-control studies are frequently employed to investigate risk factors for rare diseases, but their validity is often compromised by memory bias. This occurs when the precise recollection of past exposures differs between cases and controls, leading to inaccurate data. This distortion can be modeled as a multiplicative factor applied to the true exposure probabilities for each group. We introduce a new method that utilizes causal inference to mitigate the resulting measurement error. By leveraging the assumption of causal sufficiency, this approach estimates the bias parameters and derives the true association between disease status and exposure. The proposed technique is validated through a simulation demonstrating its effectiveness, and it is further illustrated using real-world data from a case-control investigation into the link between smoking and lung cancer.

Generative models have recently achieved remarkable success in creating synthetic data that closely resembles training samples. However, current state-of-the-art models, which rely on variational or maximum likelihood objectives, still fall short of the true maximum likelihood achievable. This limitation arises because these methods approximate the data's true distribution rather than modeling it directly. This paper introduces a new class of autoencoders capable of attaining exact maximum likelihood performance. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the optimal variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture corresponds to a self-supervised, two-layer neural network. We further show that the true maximum likelihood objective can be reached by extending these optimal VAEs with additional linear layers. Our approach involves a two-step process: first, we derive the optimal VAE by minimizing a lower bound on mutual information; second, we identify a family of linear layers that, when appended to the optimal VAE, expand the solution space to include models capable of exact maximum likelihood learning. We validate these findings through experiments on both MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets.

The exponential growth of smart city data has created a critical need for effective analysis and visualization techniques. This paper introduces a new approach that identifies correlated patterns within city data attributes, subsequently visualizing these patterns through a dynamic network graph. In this graph, nodes represent distinct patterns, while edges illustrate correlations among them. To address the inherent complexity of smart city data, we developed a specialized algorithm for mining these correlated patterns and introduced an interactive visualization method that leverages graph layout algorithms to enhance graph readability. We evaluated our approach using a real-world smart city dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in uncovering hidden correlations within the data.

This study introduces a novel, highly efficient geometric multigrid preconditioner tailored for the computational solution of generalized Stokes equations and reaction-diffusion equations utilizing the hybrid high-order (HDO)-P0 finite element method. The proposed preconditioner employs a local multigrid strategy on fine levels, where each local solver is constructed using a straightforward combination of a simple Laplacian operator and a diagonal matrix. This combination is achieved via additive Schwarz preconditioning, ensuring the resulting operator remains a diagonal modification of the multigrid preconditioner. Furthermore, the preconditioner is proven to be optimal in terms of convergence rates and is shown to be independent of the underlying mesh size. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the preconditioner is highly effective and exhibits excellent scalability across various grid resolutions.

The E-value serves as a metric to quantify how much a study's conclusions might shift if undisclosed bias were present. We then outline a method to calculate the E-value based on the posterior distribution derived from this model. Additionally, we apply this method to real-world data and demonstrate how the proposed approach can be adapted to handle not-yet-released covariates.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for handling missing data in multivariate crossover trials. The approach begins by modeling the underlying data structure and identifying the specific mechanisms driving data absence. Subsequently, it employs a multivariate imputation model to estimate missing values, followed by addressing any resulting bias through weighting techniques. The proposed method is applied to evaluate the pharmacokinetics of the oral antiretroviral drug raltegravir, specifically focusing on plasma concentrations of the drug, its active metabolite, and a key pharmacodynamic marker.

This article explores the application of functional programming to coordinate and manage virtualized network resources, specifically addressing the dynamic, multi-tenant, and multi-domain nature of these networks. It examines how functional programming languages can support the management of these complex environments, particularly in the context of the 5G era. The paper outlines the key principles for designing network architectures, covering the integration of network functions, service orchestration, and the handling of multi-tenancy. The authors argue that functional programming languages are well-suited for these tasks, as they facilitate the creation of robust, scalable, and secure network architectures. The paper concludes by summarizing the key findings and suggesting directions for future research.

This work investigates the relative efficiency of performing two-qubit versus three-qubit gates on the surface toric code. We demonstrate that any two-qubit operation can be decomposed into sequences of three-qubit gates, with the count of these gates scaling linearly with the size of the system. Consequently, three-qubit gates offer superior performance compared to two-qubit gates, a conclusion that remains valid for gate operations of higher order as well.

OPUS, the On-line Planning and Uplink System, is a web-based tool designed to manage the scheduling of observations for space telescopes. Built on the Virtual Observatory (VO) standard, OPUS offers a uniform interface for task control across various observatories, allowing users to create, modify, and delete observation requests. The system's architecture is divided into two main components: a central web interface and a backend that handles the specific requirements of each observatory. This interface enables users to define complex, multi-step observation sequences, such as simultaneous observations by multiple telescopes or follow-up observations. The backend manages interoperability by translating the standard VO task definitions into the unique task formats required by each observatory. This translation is achieved through a modular design that incorporates specific plugins for each observatory.

The paper introduces a digital learning environment designed to teach wireless networking concepts, specifically 802.11 Wi-Fi. This system integrates a real-world network emulator with a game-based approach to instruction, allowing students to study Wi-Fi protocols at a granular level. The authors report on the design and implementation of this interactive platform, alongside findings from a preliminary pilot study that assessed its effectiveness.

Ozone (O$_3$) serves as a primary method for remotely detecting molecular oxygen (O$_2$) in exoplanetary atmospheres, particularly because O$_2$ is often difficult to detect directly. This study examines the O$_2$-O$_3$ relationship within Earth-like atmospheres, specifically focusing on scenarios where both gases coexist. We demonstrate that ozone abundance in Earth's atmosphere is tightly linked to the concentration of O$_2$, a correlation that remains consistent across varying atmospheric compositions, solar flux, and orbital distances. Consequently, ozone can act as a reliable proxy for molecular oxygen in Earth-like worlds.

We investigate the Hofstadter model, defined as a lattice of non-interacting electrons subjected to a uniform magnetic field, specifically examining its surface properties. By employing a semi-infinite geometry, we demonstrate that surface currents in this system are robust against magnetic flux variations, provided the system resides within the same gap between Hofstadier minibands. This stability arises from the topological characteristics of the bulk system, which are captured by an integer-valued topological invariant. We substantiate these findings through numerical simulations, which reveal that surface currents exhibit remarkable resilience to perturbations, such as those caused by atomic-scale magnetic impurities.

This study examines how multilingual Neural Machine Interpretation (NMI) models, specifically mNMTI, can be adapted for medical use. We introduce a new mNMTI system called mNMTI-Med, which utilizes domain-adapted techniques to enhance performance in medical contexts. Our research evaluates the impact of domain adaptation on both mNMTI-Med and the standard mNMTI systems, comparing them against other methods such as standard machine translation (MTM) and mMTM, alongside traditional manual interpretation. The assessment covers various metrics, including accuracy, readability, and fluency. Results indicate that mNMTI-Med surpasses mNMTI in accuracy, readability, and fluency. Furthermore, mNMTI-Med outperforms mMTM regarding readability and fluency, and matches mMTM in accuracy. Ultimately, mNMTI-Med is the only approach that exceeds manual interpretation in terms of readability and fluency, achieving parity with manual methods in accuracy.

This study investigates the characteristics of ion-acoustic solitary waves and shock waves within a plasma comprising nonthermal electrons, a cold ion-fluid mixture, and a mobile, positively charged dust component. The analysis employs a modified Korteweg-de Vries (MKdV) equation to determine the MKdV-compact solitary wave (MKD-SW) phase speed, amplitude, and width, while utilizing the reductive perturbation technique to derive a specific MKD-SW profile. The results indicate that the MKD-SW amplitude and width are contingent upon the dust charge, whereas the phase speed relies on the dust charge, the ion fluid temperature, and the nonthermal parameter. Furthermore, the study identifies a critical dust charge threshold; exceeding this threshold renders the MKD-SW unstable. Additionally, the influence of the ion fluid temperature and nonthermal parameter on the formation of MKD-SW is examined. The paper also presents the criteria for generating altered-acoustic (ASW) shock waves and investigates how variations in the dust charge, the ion fluid and nonthermal parameters affect the ASW shock speed and compression ratio. Finally, the paper demonstrates that the dust charge and nonthermal parameter can modulate the compression ratio, thereby enabling compression ratios greater than or equal to 2.

This study introduces a new pretraining approach designed to generate compact, context-sensitive sentence embeddings for multi-language applications. The proposed method employs a specialized objective that leverages both contextual and self-supervised signals to enhance representation quality. Specifically, it utilizes an auxiliary mechanism involving a masked self-attention layer to capture local word dependencies, thereby improving the representation of individual tokens. Furthermore, the primary goal of aligning sentence embeddings with their corresponding document titles is strengthened by incorporating the context-aware auxiliary task. This dual-task strategy ensures that the embeddings are not only context-aware but also highly discriminative. The approach is evaluated on a diverse set of languages, including English, French, German, and Spanish, using the MS MARCO and MRTC benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that these context-aware, self-supervised embeddings achieve superior performance compared to existing methods across all tested languages.

Multimodal learning has gained significant traction in recent years, particularly in computer vision, where integrating information from diverse sources like images, text, and audio enhances the performance of various tasks. However, existing approaches often overlook the inherent modality-specific characteristics of data, which can lead to suboptimal outcomes. To address this, we introduce Prototypical Modal Adjustment (PMR), a novel method designed to explicitly account for these traits. PMR operates by first identifying the dominant modality for each sample and then adjusting its embedding space to align with those of the majority modality. This strategy facilitates more effective cross-modal fusion. Comprehensive experiments across multiple domains, including image classification, visual question answering, and action recognition, demonstrate that PMR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

This paper introduces a novel framework for modeling transport processes involving vector parameters, where the engagement term acts as an oriented line vector. The theory is demonstrated through a specific example: a fluid dynamics model for a two-dimensional, incompressible, active nematic system. This formulation incorporates an engagement term representing the tumbling of nematic structures within the active fluid, which is mathematically described as rotation with angular velocity proportional to the local nematic orientation. The analysis demonstrates that this tumbling effect dampens vorticity, thereby stabilizing the system.

This study introduces a Tensor-Train Network (TTN)-based approach for spoken command recognition, leveraging the TTN's ability to model high-dimensional data efficiently. The research focuses on two specific TTN configurations: the Tensor Train Network (TTN) and the Matrix Product State Network (MPSN). These models are evaluated against a baseline Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the Google Commands dataset. The results indicate that both TTN architectures surpass the CNN in performance, with TTN achieving a 90.0% accuracy and the MPSN reaching 91.1%. Furthermore, both models demonstrate superior computational efficiency compared to the CNN.

This study examines the connection between different representations of the master equation and the corresponding trajectories derived from the quantum-jump approach. By analyzing the quantum Kramers-Williams equation, we demonstrate that various equivalent forms of the master equation result in distinct jump trajectories that differ in their quantum fidelity. These fidelity differences arise from the differing degrees of non-Markovianity inherent in each representation. Furthermore, we show that, provided the system's dissipative dynamics are not too weak, one can significantly enhance the fidelity of the jumps produced by specific master equation formulations compared to others.

This study investigates the optical absorption enhancement in amorphous silicon (a-Si) thin-film solar cells by integrating gold and aluminum nanoparticles. We analyzed the influence of nanoparticle shape, size, and position on the cells' optical performance, specifically examining spherical, cylindrical, and conical geometries. Results indicate that the optimal placement of these nanoparticles is at the bottom of the thin-film layer, where they couple with the incident light to generate resonant modes. We further determined that aluminum nanoparticles with a diameter of 100 nm provide the highest enhancement in optical absorption.

This paper investigates the expressive capabilities of a first-order logic that lacks the standard evaluation (or "greatest") operator, which is typically used to select a maximal element from a defined relation. Instead, it introduces a binary choice operator capable of selecting an arbitrary element from any non-empty relation. Although this operator significantly reduces the expressive power of first-order logic with the evaluation operator, it remains sufficient to define all first-order definable queries. The study further demonstrates that extending first-order logic with this binary choice operator yields a class of queries that is strictly contained within those definable by first-order logic augmented with the evaluation operator. Finally, it is proven that these expressive limitations of first-order logic with the binary choice operator do not apply to certain extensions of such logic built upon relational algebra.

This study co-designs an energy-efficient LSTM network for video identification through hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition. The process begins by formulating a hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition algorithm, which is subsequently integrated into an LSTM network framework. The resulting LSTM architecture is then optimized via pruning and quantization algorithms to reduce energy consumption. The final results demonstrate that this approach achieves a 90.1% accuracy rate in video identification while cutting energy consumption by 30% compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

MAVLink, a communication protocol designed for unmanned systems, facilitates data exchange between aircraft and ground control stations. While widely adopted by ArduPilot and PXQ for drone operations, it currently lacks built-in security measures, leaving these systems vulnerable to attacks. This paper introduces MAVSec, a security framework that secures the MAVLink protocol by leveraging existing encryption and authentication mechanisms found in established standards like TLS and DTLS. The MAVSec architecture is built upon a layered approach, where each layer adds specific security capabilities to the protocol. This modular design allows for flexibility in implementation, enabling users to select the appropriate security level based on their specific application needs.

We introduce Kollaps, a distributed, high-performance system designed for emulating network topologies that are both dynamic and diverse. Kollaps leverages the widespread availability of commodity hardware, utilizing a distributed architecture that decouples the control plane from the data plane. This separation enables the creation of virtual network topologies that are subsequently deployed across physical infrastructures built from standard switches. The control plane manages configuration, signaling, and monitoring, while the data plane executes these instructions. The control plane itself comprises a flexible software stack featuring a dynamic topology description language, a distributed constraint solver, and a set of network-specific agents. The data plane consists of a distributed control and data forwarding system that deploys across commodity switches. This hybrid approach allows Kollaps to support a vast array of topological configurations, ranging from simple linear and mesh structures to complex hierarchical and hierarchical-leaf designs.

The Newman-Penrose formalism, a well-established framework for general relativity, utilizes a complex null tetrad to define real null directions. This work introduces a novel tetrad, termed the "realistic tetrad," which differs from the standard complex version by employing real rather than complex components. We demonstrate that a corresponding realistic variant of the Newman-Penrose mapping exists, which can be derived through a simple transformation applied to the traditional complex mapping. Furthermore, we provide a twistor-theoretic explanation for this transformation, showing that the realistic tetrad corresponds to the standard one via a pullback operation. This operation is characterized as a conformal transformation within twistor space.

This study details the design and implementation of a novel system for underground positron-electron tomography (PET) utilizing cosmic-ray muons. The system comprises a 3-meter-diameter cylindrical array of 48 plastic scintillator panels, each measuring 1 meter in length and 10 cm thick, arranged in a ring. The panels are segmented into 16 strips, 10 cm wide, and connected to a custom-built front-end electronics module. This module, built using a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), processes signals from the detectors to generate time-stamped data for every strip. The setup was deployed in the Gran Sasso Underground Laboratory, where it successfully recorded muon events. The authors present a comprehensive analysis of the system's performance, covering key metrics such as the timing resolution, spatial accuracy, and the overall detection efficiency.

Parsing expressions are a potent and intuitive approach for describing regular languages, making them highly effective for syntax analysis. However, the traditional implementations currently available are often inefficient, which can hinder their use in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a novel, highly efficient method for interpreting a restricted category of these parsing expressions. Our approach utilizes labeled lparse grammars alongside specialized data structures to achieve exceptional performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical efficacy of our method by detailing an implementation available as an open-source library.

This study examines the vacuum Cherenkov effect within a thermal environment, specifically focusing on the emission of a massless particle by a fermion moving through it. We demonstrate that the presence of a thermal bath modifies the vacuum polarization tensor, a phenomenon we term the thermal Cherenkov effect. We calculate the temperature-dependent corrections to the critical velocity required for this Cherevkov radiation and analyze the resulting particle emission rate. Our findings indicate that the finite-temperature corrections to both the critical velocity and the emission rate are negative, implying that the thermal medium suppresses the Cherevkov effect. We further examine the impact of thermal corrections on the decay of ultra-relativistic electrons in the Earth's magnetosphere, concluding that these thermal effects are negligible.

We introduce a novel method for tracking linguistic forecasts by utilizing a neural language model to quantify the probability of various spoken or written trajectories. This approach allows for the automatic detection of deviations from initial predictions and offers greater efficiency than traditional symbol-by-symbol comparison techniques. We validate this framework across three distinct scenarios: verifying data integrity in audio recordings, detecting inconsistencies in interviewee statements, and identifying shifts in political discourse. Our findings indicate that the proposed method outperforms symbol-based baselines in terms of both accuracy and processing speed.

This work introduces a novel approach to 3D object pose estimation that leverages images of the object undergoing rotation. While current methods typically rely on static inputs, they often struggle with objects in uncontrolled settings where rotation is absent. In contrast, our approach targets the prevalent scenario involving rotation—such as those found on turntables in e-commerce—by utilizing the visual changes across multiple angles to enhance estimation accuracy. We introduce a new learning framework that jointly optimizes 3D pose prediction and rotation state inference from image sequences. By modeling rotation as a continuous process, our method effectively captures the temporal evolution of rotation, enabling the recovery of high-quality pose estimates even from a single input image. We validate our approach on the ShapeNet-T dataset, demonstrating superior performance over existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines how two superconducting impurities interact within a one-dimensional electron wire, specifically focusing on the effects of crossed Andreev reflection (CAR) and elastic co-reflection (ECR). We demonstrate that the CAR and ECR processes, driven by Andreev bound states (ABSs), can be effectively controlled by adjusting the distance between the superconducting impurities. This tunability is achieved by analyzing the energy-dependent behavior of the CAR and ECR rates alongside the system's phase difference. We further show that the rates of CAR and ECR can be modulated by varying the phase difference, which is a key factor in the system. Additionally, we explore how the rates of CAR and ECR depend on the energy of the incoming electrons, noting that this energy dependence is also modulated by the phase difference. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these findings in the context of quantum computing and other technologies.

This study examines particle acceleration during magnetic reconnection within a 2D relativistic plasma, employing a hybrid approach that combines a particle-in-cell (PIC) code with a resistive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model. The PIC region is positioned at the reconnection site, while the MHD component covers the broader domain. The two models are coupled through a specialized interface that accounts for magnetic field angle-scattering, a process critical for generating the large-scale magnetic field structures necessary to drive the reconnection process. Our results indicate that this scattering mechanism is essential for particle acceleration, as it enables the formation of contracting magnetic islands that trap particles in a contracting region, thereby facilitating their acceleration. Furthermore, we observe that the efficiency of particle acceleration is strongly dependent on the spatial resolution of the PIC region and the magnitude of the scattering coefficient. Finally, our findings suggest that the mechanism of particle acceleration is consistent with previous studies, despite the differences in the numerical methods used.

This study examines how Higgs boson production via the fusion of two photons ($e^+e^- \to Zh$) and associated loop-level loop diagrams involving new particles can constrain extended scalar sectors. We specifically analyze a simplified model containing a real singlet scalar ($S$) that mixes with the Standard Model Higgs ($h$), governed by a potential $V(h,S)$. Our findings indicate that the $S$-mediated loop contribution to $e^+e^- \to Zh$ can be either constructive or destructive relative to the $h$-mediated process, depending on the sign of the $SShh$ coupling. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sensitivity of the $Zh$ channel to $S$-mediated effects is significantly enhanced compared to the corresponding contribution to the diphoton decay $h \to \gamma\gamma$. Consequently, we conclude that the $Zh$ channel offers a superior probe for detecting the $S$-mediated effects in the diphoton Higgs decay.

This paper examines the combined numerical radius, defined as the maximum of the numerical radius and its complex conjugate. We provide characterizations for the subgradients associated with this combined function, treating both the bounded case in a Hilbert space and the operator-theoretic case for bounded elements in a C*-algebra. A key outcome of this analysis is the derivation of the corresponding Lie formula for this measure.

Differential privacy (DP) has emerged as a leading technique for privacy-preserving data analysis, offering formal privacy guarantees that protect individual information. However, the current literature predominantly addresses generic DP methods, neglecting domain-specific nuances. This paper introduces a domain-adaptive DP framework tailored for financial data, which captures the unique characteristics of such information. We propose a novel DP mechanism grounded in this domain-specific understanding and provide a formal proof of its effectiveness.

This study examines the correlation between two stochastic mappings, $X$ and $Y$, where $X$ represents a random mapping from a space $A$ to a space $B$, and $Y$ represents a random mapping from a space $B$ to a space space $C$. The correlation is defined as a function of the pairings $(x, y)$, where $x \in A$ and $y \in C$. The analysis establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for $X$ and $Y$ to be uncorrelated, alongside an examination of correlation transitivity. The paper further introduces the concept of random dispersion fields, defined as the collection of correlations between $X$ and $Y$ as $Y$ varies. The discussion concludes by linking these dispersion fields to the theory of random mappings.

This study examines the initiation of high-pressure H₂-O₂-He-O₂ combustible mixtures using unfocused laser beams. The research investigates how varying the initial temperature, pressure, and laser intensity affects the ignition delay time. A key finding is that the ignition delay time exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with the initial temperature, a phenomenon attributed to the complex interplay between thermal and chemical mechanisms. Additionally, the impact of adding helium on laser ignition is analyzed, specifically regarding how it alters the thermal properties of the gas mixture. The results indicate that incorporating helium significantly reduces laser ignition delay times, a effect driven by changes in the thermal diffusivity of the gas.

This study introduces a new approach for image segmentation that delivers high accuracy across various applications, including medical imaging, while maintaining computational efficiency for mobile devices. The method employs a dual-branch architecture designed to extract features from both the center and the periphery of an image, addressing the often-overlooked importance of boundary regions. To further enhance performance, we developed a specialized loss function that integrates boundary-aware supervision, which significantly improves segmentation quality. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on standard benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we validated its practical utility by deploying it on both web platforms and mobile devices, confirming its effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

This paper introduces a collaborative driver messenger system (CDA) designed to enhance a vehicle's rear view by utilizing on-board sensors and inter-vehicle communication. The system captures rear images, applies image processing techniques to identify and track objects, and transmits their data to neighboring vehicles via a CDA. These vehicles then display the received information on their in-vehicle displays. The study details the CDA's architecture, including the implementation of a communication protocol and the development of a user interface for a test bench. Furthermore, it presents a simulation of a real-world scenario to demonstrate the system's functionality.

This study examines the Brownian movement of noninteracting weakly active particles within diverse geometric configurations, specifically accounting for the influence of boundaries. By employing the method of images, we derive the two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) time-dependent probability density functions for particle positions. Our analysis reveals that the mean squared displacement (MSD) of these particles is non-monotonic with respect to the time scale, a characteristic that transitions from subdiffusive to superdiffusive regimes. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of wall proximity on the motility of these active particles, demonstrating that the wall-induced enhancement of their mean squared velocity is more pronounced in three dimensions compared to two.

The mechanism is defined by a specific Hamiltonian, which is solved using the Bethe ansatz. The resulting solution reveals a duality between the system's parameters and those of a corresponding model featuring particle repulsion. Furthermore, the analysis derives the ground state energy, the ground state wave function, and the spectrum of excited states. This study presents an analysis of the rapid variability in Si IV emission at a sub-second cadence during a solar flare. Utilizing data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), we examined the temporal evolution of the Si IV 1402.77 \AA{} spectral line at a specific flare site. Our analysis reveals that the line's full width at half maximum (FWHM) fluctuates significantly on a sub-second timescale, with peak-to-peak variations reaching up to 100 km. These rapid shifts in spectral line width are interpreted as evidence of dynamic flows within the flare's chromosphere. Furthermore, we observed a strong correlation between the line width and the intensity of the spectral continuum, suggesting that the mechanisms driving flow dynamics are closely linked to flare heating processes. These findings offer valuable insights into the temporal behavior of flows in flaring regions and their relationship with the heating mechanisms of the chromosphere.

The Standard Model of particle physics faces a significant hurdle known as the strong CP problem, which remains unresolved. While axions were originally proposed as CP-violating solutions, they have since emerged as leading dark matter candidates. This article examines the theoretical foundations of the axion, its current experimental status, and its potential implications for the dark matter enigma.

This study examines the influence of collision cascade dynamics on the critical angle for nanopatterning induced by ion irradiation in thin films. The analysis focuses on the specific mechanisms of cascade events that lead to material removal, specifically through the formation of a "nanopitted" surface. The authors demonstrate that the probability of such a surface forming is governed by the ratio of the maximum projected ion path length to the surface layer thickness, while the critical angle is determined by the ratio of the surface layer thickness to the maximum projected ion path length. The maximum projected ion path length is calculated as the sum of the projected ion range and the projected distance from the surface to the deepest point of the collision cascade. The software community is increasingly concerned with anti-plagiarism, a challenge that is becoming more complex as code is increasingly written in the cloud. This paper introduces a new approach to anti-plagiarism, which we term "pathways." A code similarity measure is derived by analyzing the shortest paths in code dependency graphs, which are constructed from the code's abstract syntax trees. We provide a proof-of-concept implementation in C#, which we have made publicly available. Initial tests indicate that this method is effective, and we anticipate that it can be easily adapted to other programming languages.

This paper investigates the complete convergence of Dirichlet series of automorphic origin, deriving sufficient conditions for such convergence based on the growth of automorphic L-functions within vertical strips. These conditions are expressed through moments of automorphic L-functions, yielding novel results applicable to classical modular forms, Hecke-Maforms, and certain non-holomorphic Maforms of weight 2.

This study examines the properties of metric near subgroups within metric groups, focusing specifically on the interplay between their metric and algebraic characteristics. We demonstrate that if a metric group possesses a metric near subgroup $H$, then the large-scale (coarse) structure of $ G $ is fundamentally determined by that of $ G/H $, thereby establishing a correspondence between the unbounded 2-point distances in $ G $ and those in $ G/H $. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between metric near subgroups and centralizers, proving that any maximal near subgroup that is quasi-isometrically embedded possesses a centralizer that is also a near subgroup. Additionally, we show that the maximal near subgroups within the unit sphere of a non-elementary hyperbolic group are precisely the elliptic maximal tori. Finally, we outline a generalization of the concept of near subgroups to the realm of topological groups.

This study introduces a novel computational system for estimating log-conconcave densities, built upon an innovative algorithm that efficiently solves the underlying convex optimization problem. The method's performance is evaluated against existing approaches, demonstrating that it achieves superior precision and precision in confidence interval estimation. Furthermore, the technique is applied to analyze real-world data, specifically a dataset of 1,000 birth weights collected from the University of North Carolina.

This study introduces a novel Wang-Landau-based entropic sampling method designed to determine the entropy of static granular systems. By modeling the system as a collection of rigid blocks with specified shapes and sizes, we investigate the entropy of microstates defined by the positions of these blocks. We demonstrate that the entropy of a configuration is equivalent to the count of rigid-body translations and rotations permitted by the rigid motions of its constituent blocks. This approach enables the calculation of the entropy for any microstate, provided the total count of rigid motions is known. We apply this method to analyze the entropy of microstates in static granular systems at various volume densities. Our results indicate that the entropy of a microstate is not solely dependent on the system's volume but also on the number of constituent blocks. This paper introduces a new game-theoretic framework defined on graphs, in which two players, an "adventurer director" and a "producer," vie for control over a directed graph. The producer seeks to maximize the graph's connectivity by adding edges, while the adventurer-director aims to minimize it by removing them. We demonstrate that the specific set of subgraphs that remain stable under this dynamic corresponds exactly to those satisfying a particular 3-local property, a finding that leads to a polynomial-time algorithm for identifying them. Our analysis further reveals connections to the producer's optimization problem, specifically the problem of finding a maximum spanning tree, and we establish the computational complexity of determining the winner for various restricted graph categories.

This study examines the frequency-frequency relationships of single-trajectory spectral densities (SSDs) within Gaussian processes, which are crucial for characterizing the stochastic dynamics of mesoscopic systems. SSDs are derived from the statistical properties of individual trajectories and are essential for analyzing time series data. We demonstrate that SSDs for Gaussian processes can be expressed as a sum of Gaussian spectral densities, where the parameters of these components are determined by the process's autocorrelation function. Furthermore, we show that the shape of the SSD's frequency-frequency relationship is governed by the distribution of these parameters. Consequently, this distribution can be reconstructed from SSDs obtained from experimental data, thereby providing insight into the underlying stochastic dynamics.

This study investigates the (1+1)-dimensional higher-order Broer-Kaup system utilizing the nonlinear superposition framework. By establishing the system's integrability through the construction of an auto-Bäcklund transformation and a Lax pair, researchers derived its solutions through the interaction of solitons. Furthermore, graphical representations were employed to analyze the properties of these solitonic interactions.

This work examines the weak solutions to the incompressible Euler equations, defined by the system:
$$
\partial_t \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{v} + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0,
$$
where $\mathbf{v}$ represents the velocity field and $p$ is the pressure. We demonstrate that, provided the velocity field $\mathbf{v}$ is a distributional solution with square-integrable vorticity $\omega = \nabla\times\mathbf{v}$, the $L^2$ norm of $\mathbf{v}$ remains constant over time. This proof relies on the property that the vorticity also evolves as a distributional solution.

The Virtual Illusion Universe Project (VIRUP) is a novel initiative designed to create a virtual reality experience of the cosmos, intended to be accessible via the Internet. This project will utilize a dynamic, three-dimensional simulation of the universe, where the positions and movements of all objects are governed by the Lambda Cold Dark Matter model. This simulation will rely on the latest data from galaxy surveys, weak lensing, and cosmic microwave background radiation. VIRUP aims to provide an immersive, educational, and interactive platform for exploring the cosmos, with the ultimate goal of becoming a publicly accessible resource for education and research.

We introduce a method for introducing data science to children by utilizing the Data Bricks Space Voyage (DBSV) dataset, which contains space exploration records from NASA. This effort involves creating a data visualization tool that converts the raw information into tangible objects, enabling young learners to interact with the data through a hands-on experience. Additionally, a data literacy curriculum has been developed to guide children in analyzing patterns within the dataset. Our approach is designed to be adaptable for various age groups, and we are currently conducting a pilot study to evaluate the tool and curriculum, with the goal of refining the experience based on feedback.

Software Defined Networking (SDN) has emerged as a transformative paradigm for network management, offering enhanced programmability and flexibility. However, the extensive configuration space within SDN-driven control planes has led to a surge in operational issues. To address this, researchers have developed various tools for analyzing control plane configurations, yet these tools often fail to account for the actual operational constraints imposed by the data-plane. This paper introduces a methodology to identify operational constraints within control plane configurations by leveraging data-plane state information. Specifically, we utilize data-plane state snapshots to extract the set of active flows and map them to corresponding rules in the control plane configuration. This mapping reveals which rules are essential for maintaining current data-plane functionality. We demonstrate the practical application of this approach through two use cases: (1) detecting control plane configurations that are incompatible with specific data-plane states, and (2) identifying control plane configurations that are redundant.

Disentangled representations are crucial for various downstream tasks, including representation learning, transfer learning, and causal inference. However, current approaches often fail to leverage relational data, which is prevalent in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to learn weakly disentangled representations by explicitly incorporating relational information. Our method employs a new disentanglement metric that accounts for the interplay between object attributes and their spatial relationships. Furthermore, we utilize a relational graph convolutional network to capture these spatial interactions. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the hydrodynamic interactions between tandem oscillating foils, specifically analyzing how various parameters influence wake energy recovery. We demonstrate that the phase difference between foils dictates the nature of these interactions, which can be either constructive or destructive. Constructive interactions facilitate the generation of high-velocity jets, whereas destructive ones result in low-velocity jets. Furthermore, we establish a correlation between wake characteristics and the performance of the second foil, showing that the second device achieves peak efficiency when the wake velocity is minimal. This finding is confirmed through a comparison of experimental data and numerical simulations, which reveal that the vortex shedding frequency of the first foil is the primary factor governing the wake velocity.

We examine the application of Bayesian inference techniques to reconstruct real-time dynamics within Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). By utilizing a Bayesian framework, we demonstrate that the real-time evolution of the QCD quark condensate can be accurately reconstructed from Euclidean correlators defined at finite temperature. This analysis relies on a combined approach employing both perturbative and nonperturbative methods. Specifically, we show that the resulting real-time dynamics can be recovered with high precision by integrating perturbative constraints at high energies with nonperturbative insights at low energies.

We introduce a methodology for investigating electron tunneling dynamics between a quantum dot and a superconducting island. This approach utilizes a gate electrode to monitor the quantum dot's charge state, with the gate capacitance varying according to the superconducting island's charge parity. By analyzing these capacitance fluctuations, we can deduce the specific charge-tunneling rates. This technique is particularly valuable for examining systems where direct measurement of tunneling rates is otherwise difficult.

Simulating drug-target interactions is a critical step in drug discovery, yet it remains computationally demanding. While deep generative models have shown promise in generating novel drug candidates, they often struggle with poor interpretability and a lack of control over specific properties. To address these limitations, we introduce a generative framework for drug-target pair simulation that is both efficient and controllable. Our approach utilizes a drug-target interaction energy model to evaluate binding affinity and incorporates a multi-objective optimization framework to steer the generation of drug-target pairs toward targets of interest. We validate this method by generating molecules capable of binding to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease.

The Graph of Interaction mechanisms, similar to the CEGIS algorithm, operate on a token-based guidance system. We propose a novel approach to the Dynamic Graph of Interaction (DGI) that employs a token-based, directed graph structure. Our work introduces a novel token-based directed graph structure, the Dynamic Graph of Interaction (DGI), which integrates the token-based guidance principles of the CEGIS algorithm with a token-based directed graph structure. The DGI leverages the token-based guidance strategy inherent to the CEGIS algorithm,

We present proper motion measurements for the outer regions of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), derived from the VLT Survey Telescope's VMC project. This analysis utilizes a sample of 1,013 LMC member stars, including 102 blue stragglers, 90 blue hooks, and 800 blue main sequence stars. The resulting proper motion is $\mu_{\rm N} = -0.11 \pm 0.02$ mas yr$^{-1}$ and $\mu_{\rm E} = -0.09 \pm 0.02$ mas yr$^{-1}$. These values indicate that the outer LMC is moving away from the Galactic plane at a velocity of $-10.2 \pm 3.2$ km s$^{-1}$. Furthermore, we observe a strong correlation between proper motion and distance, suggesting that the LMC's motion is influenced by the SMC. This interaction is consistent with a scenario where the LMC and SMC are co-orbital satellites of the Milky Way, moving in opposite directions.

Power theft detection in Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) networks is a critical task for utilities, as it safeguards their financial interests. While recent studies have applied deep learning to this challenge, they often rely on fixed hyperparameters, which can lead to suboptimal performance. This paper introduces a random tuning hyperparameter strategy designed to enhance the accuracy of deep learning-based theft detection. The method involves training multiple models with varying hyperparameters and selecting the best performer based on a validation dataset. We evaluated this approach using data from 1,000 smart meters in a real-world setting, comparing it against a standard deep learning baseline. Results indicate that random hyperparameter tuning yields an accuracy improvement of 1.5% to 2.5% over the fixed-parameter model.

We introduce a novel inductive methodology for constructing topological invariants related to marked compact surface groups. This approach is demonstrated through the derivation of a new formula for the Gassner map's components, which are defined as collections of power series.

This study reports the first simultaneous measurement of the lifetimes for the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons, utilizing the $\to K^- p \pi^+$ and $\to K^- K^0 \pi^+$ decay modes, respectively. Data were collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of 7, 8, and 13 TeV, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb$^{-1}$. The observed lifetimes are $\tau(\Omega^{0}_{c}) = 0.0590^{+0.0054}_{-0.0050}$ ps and $\tau(\Xi^{0}_{c}) = 1.526^{+0.019}_{-0.018}$ ps. These results align with the predictions of the Quark Model.

Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification is a critical task in remote sensing, yet it remains challenging due to the high dimensionality of spectral data and the scarcity of labeled samples. While subspace clustering (SC) offers a promising solution by leveraging the subspace structure of HSIs, existing SC methods often fail to achieve optimal performance because they neglect the unique characteristics of HSI data. To address this, we introduce a rapid and accurate similarity-constrained subspace framework for SC. First, we employ a similarity-constrained mechanism to capture the intrinsic correlations between adjacent pixels, thereby enhancing the representation of HSI data. Second, we integrate a new similarity constraint to further improve the representation capability of SC. Third, we implement a scalable alternating optimization algorithm to ensure computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both classification accuracy and processing speed.

This study introduces a simplified model designed to simulate snow accumulation on sea ice, specifically targeting the formation of snow ridges. The model incorporates snow advection driven by wind and the subsequent sublimation of snow under calm conditions. It reveals that the interaction between wind-driven snow transport and ice surface topography generates localized snow ridges. These ridges are characterized by sharp snow peaks aligned with the wind trajectory, separated by deep troughs. The model accurately reproduces the spatial distribution of snow ridges observed in Arctic sea ice areas, such as the Laptev Sea, and predicts that these ridges become more pronounced as wind speeds increase.

We investigate the scattering of cold atoms and molecules within a dynamically oscillating magnetic field. Our analysis reveals that the scattering cross-section is subject to the quantum Zeno effect, a phenomenon that can be sustained indefinitely through an oscillation frequency exceeding a critical threshold. Furthermore, we identify a "critical frequency" that marks a transition from a non-Zeno to a Zeno regime. Notably, this critical frequency is not constant but varies with scattering length, scattering angle, and the strength of the magnetic field. Additionally, under specific conditions, the scattering cross-section exhibits resonant peaks, indicating a "resonant Zeno effect." These findings demonstrate that dynamic magnetic fields serve as a powerful instrument for controlling ultracold atom-molecule scattering processes.

This study examines the connection between nonextensive Tsallis entropy and the It\^o-Langevin framework, which governs the stochastic dynamics of Brownian particles. We establish a novel Langevin equation characterized by a nonextensive derivative, which controls the time-dependent evolution of a Brownian particle's mean position. This formulation is derived from a nonextensive Fokker-Planck equation, where itself originates from a corresponding nonextensive stochastic It\^o-Langevin equation. Furthermore, we derive a new expression for Tsallis entropy applicable to the probability density functions of the stochastic processes described by this nonextensive Langevin equation.

The optical generation of Floquet states within a nodal-line semimetal allows for the creation of higher-order Weyl nodes, which serve as the foundation for topological surface states. This study investigates the optical generation of such a semimetal, revealing that applying a periodic modulation to the electric field induces a transformation from a nodal-line into a nodal-loop and nodal-Weyl configurations. This process produces four-fold degenerate Weyl nodes along with pairs of Weyl nodes possessing a Chern number of $\pm2$. While the surface states associated with the degenerate nodes remain trivial, those linked to the Chern nodes exhibit a nontrivial character. These nontrivial states are identified as higher-order topological states, distinguished by the presence of one-dimensional chiral edge modes at the sample boundaries.

Distributed computing has emerged as a powerful approach for tackling complex problems, yet it faces significant hurdles regarding data security and the efficient distribution of rewards. To address these issues, we introduce Marvel, a decentralized framework that leverages idle computing resources to securely solve distributed problems while ensuring contributors are fairly compensated. Marvel offers several key advantages: it employs a blockchain to guarantee transparency and traceability, utilizes a novel resource verification mechanism to ensure data security, and implements a reward allocation strategy designed to motivate participants. Additionally, Marvel is highly scalable, allowing for the dynamic addition of resources to meet varying computational demands. We have also developed Marvel DC, a distributed cloud protocol that integrates Marvel's capabilities with the capabilities of the Internet of Things (IoT) to enable secure, distributed data processing. Experimental results indicate that Marvel DC surpasses existing solutions in both performance and efficiency.

This paper introduces a reduced-reference perceptual quality framework designed for the rate control of 3D point cloud compression. The approach begins by deriving a rate-distortion function for point clouds, followed by the development of a distortion metric that quantifies the visual degradation caused by rate-distortion trade-offs. The resulting model is validated through experiments on the MPEG-PCC reference software, demonstrating strong alignment with subjective quality assessments. Leveraging this validated model, the study proposes a new rate control strategy that surpasses the performance of the existing method in the MPEG-PCC standard.

We employ the gauge/gravity duality to investigate the phase diagram of strongly coupled QCD under the influence of finite temperature and chemical potential. Our analysis indicates that holographic QCD predicts a reentrant phase transition within the region of high density and low chemical potential.

This paper introduces a self-supervised learning (SSL) framework designed to address the scarcity of labeled data in anomaly detection for knee magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed method leverages a Transformer-based architecture that incorporates patch-wise self-attention and contrastive learning to generate robust feature representations. By utilizing a dual-encoder structure, the model extracts features from both the input and augmented versions of each MRI slice. This approach is particularly effective for detecting abnormalities in knee MRI scans, where labeling is expensive and time-consuming. Experimental results on a large-scale, publicly available knee MRI dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms other SSL approaches and achieves performance comparable to models trained with labels.

This study introduces a deep learning approach for few-shot typography generation, tackling the challenge of creating new font styles from minimal samples. While previous methods typically rely on global glyph shapes, our work emphasizes the critical role of local style details, such as stroke thickness and line curvature, in font design. We propose a framework that utilizes a set of local style features to design a generative network capable of synthesizing a comprehensive font from a few examples. Additionally, we have created a novel dataset comprising 1,000 typefaces, each with over 100 glyphs, to support our experiments. Empirical results demonstrate that our method successfully generates high-quality fonts across various alphabets and styles, effectively outperforming existing approaches.

This study examines the impact of chiral torsion on the equation of state for a relativistic, charged, chiral fermion plasma in thermal equilibrium. We demonstrate that the torsion field induces a chiral magnetic effect, resulting in a non-zero current even when the system is at rest. Furthermore, we analyze the equation of state across varying torsion field intensities, identifying a critical threshold beyond which the system transitions from a stable fluid phase to a spinor condensate.

This study introduces a novel, user-specific strategy for enhancing the quality of experience (QoE) within adaptive video streaming. The proposed method leverages digital twins to forecast individual quality preferences and dynamically adjusts streaming bitrate based on real-time network conditions. The system's efficacy is evaluated through a comprehensive simulation framework, comparing its performance against baseline approaches that rely on fixed or purely adaptive bitrate selection. The results demonstrate that the user-specific scheme achieves superior perceived video quality compared to these traditional methods.

This study details a specific double waterfall algorithm designed for KM3NeT/ARCA, intended for reconstructing double cascade events. The method utilizes a two-stage approach: an initial, fast coarse reconstruction followed by a refined step that calculates the precise 3D coordinates for every secondary particle. We evaluate the algorithm's performance regarding position accuracy, impact point determination, and energy estimation. Furthermore, we examine the effects of varying the number of hits used in the reconstruction process.

This study investigates the periodic nonlinear Schrödinger equation perturbed by random noise in the dispersion, where the initial data are deterministic but bounded within a Sobolev space $H^s([0,L]\times\mathbb{R}^d)$ with $s>d/2$. We establish that the resulting random Cauchy problem possesses a unique global solution defined for all time almost surely. Furthermore, the solution demonstrates uniform regularity over the spatial periodic domain and satisfies a specific decay condition as $|x|$ increases, holding almost surely.

This study examines a wireless communication system featuring a transmitter and a receiver connected by $K$ parallel links. The objective is to achieve reliable communication with a guaranteed latency limit, accounting for the fact that each link may experience packet erasures. To address this, we propose a joint design that optimizes both coding strategies and resource allocation. Specifically, we develop a novel class of codes termed "joint allocation and coding" (JAC). The process begins by assigning transmission probabilities to individual links; subsequently, messages are encoded and distributed across these links using erasure codes. This approach allows the receiver to reconstruct the original message once a sufficient quantity of successfully transmitted packets is gathered. The allocation and coding scheme are jointly optimized to satisfy the latency and reliability constraints while maximizing the system's throughput. The paper further analyzes the theoretical limits of these schemes, providing both lower and upper bounds on their performance. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to evaluate the proposed JAC methods and demonstrate their effectiveness.

Sgr A East, the supernova remnant located at the center of the Milky Way, is a unique object that has long puzzled astronomers. Its formation is thought to involve a massive star that exploded roughly 2–3 million years ago, leaving behind a remnant that has since expanded to a radius of approximately 3 parsecs. This study utilizes a new method to determine the progenitor's birth location, a critical step in reconstructing the event's history. By analyzing the remnant's current position and motion, along with the trajectories of nearby molecular clouds, we can identify the site of the original explosion. Our results indicate that the progenitor star originated near the Galactic center, situated within a few parsecs of the supermassive black hole Sgr A*. This proximity suggests the star was part of a dense, massive cluster that formed in situ. The supernova's blast likely triggered the formation of the nearby molecular clouds, which now exhibit a distinct "shattered filament" structure. This study also demonstrates that the kinematic data of the remnant and surrounding clouds can be used to estimate the age of the supernova.

Recent findings from the LHCb collaboration regarding deviations in the $R_{\text{c}}$ and $R_{\text{c}}$ ratios have prompted significant interest in the lepton universality sector. This study revisits these anomalies through a comprehensive phenomenological framework, utilizing a two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) with Type II Yukawa couplings. We demonstrate that the observed discrepancies can be explained by loop-level contributions from charged Higgs bosons, provided the model adheres to the Standard Model's particle content and gauge interactions. Furthermore, we analyze the model's compatibility with existing experimental data and its predictive potential for forthcoming measurements.

This paper presents our contribution to the DISRPT 2021 Shared Task, detailing our methodologies for three specific sub-tasks: discourse unit segmentation, discourse categorization, and connective classification. For the segmentation task, we employed a rule-based approach that achieved the highest performance on the public development set, securing a spot in the final leaderboard. For the categorization sub-task, our system utilized a neural network trained on the DISRPT 19 Shared Task's public development set, which yielded the top-ranked result on the final leaderboard. Finally, for the connective detection task, our approach relied on a rule-based method that identified 1,000 out of the 2,000 gold-standard labels on the public development set, correctly classifying 1,000 instances.

The Internet of Everything (IoE) is poised to revolutionize the Internet of Things (IoT) by enabling the seamless interconnection of diverse systems, including humans, machines, and the physical world. This expansion is expected to generate massive data volumes, necessitating the integration of cloud, fog, and edge computing to ensure efficient data processing. However, the heightened complexity of IoE introduces significant challenges, particularly regarding security and privacy. Consequently, there is an urgent need for robust security and privacy mechanisms to protect IoE users and their data. This paper introduces a Blockchain-enabled Accountable Clear Infrastructure Sharing (BEAT) framework designed to address these challenges. By leveraging blockchain technology, BEAT facilitates transparent and accountable infrastructure sharing, thereby enhancing the security and privacy of IoE users. The study further presents a comprehensive blockchain-based architecture for IoE, outlining essential security and privacy protocols. Finally, the paper details a comprehensive IoE security and privacy model, providing specific guidelines for safeguarding user data.

The Okubo-Weiss criterion serves as a widely recognized diagnostic tool for identifying regions within a two-dimensional flow where the non-linear advection of vorticity is dominant over stretching. This study examines the Okubo-Weiss criterion across various two-dimensional fluid systems, including the Euler, Navier-Stokes, and MHD equations, as well as the shallow water equations, and the 2D-Quasi-Geostrophic equations. We demonstrate that the Okubo-Weiss criterion can be generalized to any two-dimensional flow system that satisfies a specific set of requirements. Furthermore, we establish that the criterion can be expressed in terms of the vorticity gradient and the vorticity Laplacian, revealing a strong parallel to the Okubo-Weiss formulation for the Navier-Stokes equations.

This study examines the thermodynamics of Lee-Wick (Lee-Wick) bosons, focusing specifically on the early universe's cosmology. We demonstrate that the thermal bath of these bosons, which is typically assumed to be decoupled from the Hubble expansion, can instead drive the universe's expansion. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of this mechanism for the Hubble parameter and the cosmic scale factor.

This paper introduces a novel method for transferring artistic styles between images using a Transformer-based architecture. Unlike previous approaches that rely on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), our method leverages the Transformer's ability to model long-range dependencies, thereby capturing style information more effectively. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through two style translation tasks: first, translating images into the style of famous artworks, and second, performing style translation between artworks themselves. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing techniques in both tasks. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/Chenrui-888/StyTr2.

The concept of thermodynamic length, which quantifies the total number of microscopic configurations in a system, has recently been applied to characterize the efficiency of thermodynamic protocols. This study demonstrates that for a fixed change in a system's thermodynamic length, erasure processes achieve a constant dissipation rate that is superior to any other heat engine cycle. We validated this principle experimentally using a colloidal particle within a time-varying optical trap. Furthermore, we show that while the total work required for a procedure remains fixed when defined by thermodynamic length, the associated entropy production fluctuates significantly depending on the speed at which the system's state is traversed.

This study examines the stability of nonuniform fluids subjected to acoustic fields, utilizing the Boussinesq approximation to model the governing equations. The analysis reveals that the system exhibits a symmetry between gravity and the acoustic field, which can be leveraged to simplify the governing equations. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the acoustic field's influence on the system's stability is contingent upon the fluid's initial state.

This paper investigates the analytic characteristics of commuting, isometric, and algebraic properties of weighted shifts within generalized directed semi-trees. It establishes a structural theorem for these shifts, defines a novel invariant known as the Toeplitz matrix, and outlines the complete validity conditions for their respective properties. Furthermore, it presents necessary and sufficient criteria determining when such shifts belong to the Volterra class.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a standard approach for processing graph-structured data, yet their performance is often hindered by the inability to capture the full spectrum of gate diversity and their inability to identify critical subgraphs. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel GCN variant that enhances gate diversity and incorporates attention mechanisms to prioritize important graph regions. Furthermore, we propose a new metric for assessing the syntactic significance of subgraphs, which facilitates the detection of optimal subgraphs for classification. Experimental results on three graph classification benchmarks demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 3.5%.

This work examines the geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers within a regression framework characterized by errors in both dependent and independent variables. By employing standard techniques for parameter estimation in such models, we demonstrate that the sampler exhibits geometric ergodicity provided the coefficient of the independent variable is nonzero.

This study introduces a new multi-qubit control framework designed to enhance sensing capabilities in the presence of noise. We examine a system of $N$ qubits governed by a Heisenberg exchange interaction, where the goal is to determine an optimal control sequence that maximizes the Fisher information associated with a parameter $\theta$ imprinted on the collective state. We assume the parameter is subject to uncertainty, modeled as a random variable with a known distribution. Consequently, the control strategy must be robust, ensuring high sensitivity to $\theta$ across the entire range of its possible values. We demonstrate that this problem can be formulated as a constrained optimization task and solved using the multi-start approach. This method involves generating numerous random initial conditions for the gradient ascent algorithm, each yielding a distinct final state. By evaluating the Fisher information for each resulting state across the full spectrum of $\theta$, we identify the one offering the highest average sensitivity. We validate this approach on a three-qubit system under various noise conditions, showing that the derived robust control strategy consistently achieves superior sensitivity compared to alternative methods.

This study introduces a novel methodology for analyzing nonlinear dynamical systems subject to random noise. By utilizing a nonlinear extension of the Koopman operator framework, the approach represents both linear and nonlinear components as infinite-dimensional linear operators. Consequently, the resulting linear stochastic equation of motion is solved using the standard Krylov subspacetechnique. This strategy enables the derivation of nonlinear normal modes and the calculation of the stochastic equivalent linearization (SEL) matrix. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through its application to a Duffing oscillator, with a specific focus on determining the stability of the resulting eigenmodes.

This study examines the propagation of a monochromatic point source within a three-dimensional scattering medium characterized by nonlinear absorption. The interaction between the nonlinear absorption coefficient and the scattering mean free path is defined by a dimensionless parameter, $\alpha$. When $\alpha$ is small, the system operates in a weakly nonlinear regime where the intensity profile is governed by a modified Bessel function of the first kind, $I_0$. In contrast, for large $\alpha$, the intensity profile transitions to a Gaussian form, resembling that of a ballistic wave. The transition between these two distinct behaviors occurs at a critical value of $\alpha$ that is proportional to the ratio of the wavelength to the mean free path.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved remarkable success in numerous domains, including game playing, robotics, and autonomous driving. However, these advancements have come at the cost of reduced transparency, making it difficult for humans to comprehend the agent's reasoning and actions. This lack of interpretability is particularly concerning in high-stakes fields where understanding the agent's decision-making process is essential. This paper reviews current research on RL interpretability, focusing on methods that offer high levels of transparency. We begin by outlining RL fundamentals and relevant background concepts, followed by a detailed examination of various interpretation techniques. We conclude by summarizing the primary challenges in the field and identifying promising future research directions.

This work examines the single-variable logic framework for lattices, denoted as $L\text{-}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{L}$, and establishes a categorical duality between its algebraic semantics and a specific category of functors derived from the category of frames for $L\text{-}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{L}$. Leveraging this connection, the study introduces a new class of $L\text{-}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{L}$-algebras known as $L$-flat algebras, which are characterized by the fact that they are defined by their underlying frame structures.

This study examines the localization accuracy of 5G cellular networks operating in the millimeter-wave spectrum. We introduce a statistical framework designed to characterize and analyze the performance of Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) and Ranging Time of Arrival (RTOA) based methods. Our findings indicate that, for a specific target node, the observed time difference of arrivals exhibits a Gaussian distribution, whereas the ranging measurement residual follows a Gamma distribution. Furthermore, we derive the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) for these methods and determine its asymptotic variance, which serves as a metric for estimation accuracy. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed statistical models and the proposed estimators are highly accurate, particularly when the number of base stations is substantial.
We introduce a novel method for generating a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate within the Gross-Pitaevskii limit, employing just a single optical dipole trap.

Image inpainting involves reconstructing missing or corrupted areas within an image. Although deep learning has recently achieved significant success in this domain, most current methods struggle with high-resolution inputs, often failing to generate realistic textures and fine details. To address this, we introduce a novel two-tier deep learning framework designed for high-resolution image inpainting. This approach first employs a pre-trained GAN-based upscaling model to convert a high-resolution image into a high-resolution latent space, followed by a dedicated inpainting network that fills in the gaps within this latent representation. The entire system is trained end-to-end, leveraging a pre-trained VAE for the encoding stage and the pre-trained GAN for upscaling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, successfully restoring intricate textures and details in high-resolution imagery.

This paper investigates a novel bandit problem where the optimal arm is defined by a threshold on the expected rewards of all arms, and crucially, the mean reward of every arm is a linear function of a shared, unknown parameter. This framework encompasses numerous real-world scenarios, such as selecting the most effective treatment for patients with varying baseline health risks, where the treatment effect is additive to that baseline. We propose a solution strategy that leverages the structural dependencies among arms to identify the optimum with high efficiency. Our approach achieves regret rates that are superior to those of leading existing methods, even in the absence of such structural information.
